data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is true or probable, but as a critical-rational decision to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby minimizing the risk of known error without assuming future regularity.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the choice of action requires a positive guarantee of success (e.g., life-critical engineering where 'not yet falsified' is insufficient), the Popperian stance collapses into practical skepticism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'severity' of tests cannot be objectively defined independent of the theory being tested, the ranking of corroboration becomes circular.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent implicitly assumes that nature is uniform enough that passing past tests matters for future actions, they have smuggled in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction) and 'critical preference' (which relies on negative knowledge). By treating corroboration as a report of past performance under stress rather than a predictor of future success, the agent adopts the best-tested theory because it is the only one whose errors have been actively sought and not yet found. This shifts the burden from proving the theory right to acknowledging that alternatives have been proven wrong or are less tested. The preference is a methodological rule for error avoidance, not an epistemic claim about probability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
